files.feeds/browser/x-orbital-lab/feed.yaml:
title: 'X: Orbital Lab'
suffix: x-orbital-lab
# A fictional profile page (demo/sites/x.html, served by tools/record_demo.py). Its posts are drawn by a script
# and more load on scrolling, as on x.com, so x.py reads it in Camoufox. For a real profile, use its address and
# a browser profile signed in to X: params: {profile: x}, then ./firefox-profile.sh x https://x.com
source: https://gchristensen.github.io/feedxcavator/demo/sites/x.html
tags: [browser]
extractor: x-profile
selectors:
  item: 'article[data-testid=tweet]'
  title: '[data-testid=tweetText]'
  summary: '[data-testid=tweetText]'
  link: 'a[href*="/status/"]'
  image: '[data-testid=tweetPhoto] img'
  published: {css: 'time::attr(datetime)', parse: date}
tasks: [browser]
files.feeds/browser/x-screenshots/feed.yaml:
title: 'X: Orbital Lab, as pictures'
suffix: x-screenshots
# Each post as a screenshot, so quotes, polls and cards look as they do on X. Needs a browser profile signed
# in to X: ./firefox-profile.sh x https://x.com. Not recorded: the demo shows an output written by hand
# (frontend/src/demo/handmade/x-screenshots.xml).
source: https://x.com/orbital_lab
tags: [browser]
extractor: x-screenshots
params: {profile: x}
output: {limit: 10}
# Posts as pictures: posts.js finds the posts on the page, then each one is screenshotted and kept in the # image store (/image/), and the headline shows the picture. from html import escape # hidden while a shot is taken: the sticky bars that would lie over the post HIDE = "[data-testid=TopNavBar], [data-testid=BottomBar] {visibility: hidden !important}" @extractor("x-screenshots") def x_screenshots(feed): with browser(profile=feed.params["profile"]) as b: page = b.open(feed.source, wait_for="article[data-testid=tweet]", timeout=60) headlines = [] for post in page.evaluate(load_js("posts"), 10): shot = page.screenshot(post["selector"], type="jpeg", quality=85, style=HIDE) image = store_image(shot, "image/jpeg", post["link"]) headlines.append({ "title": post["text"][:100] or "(a post without text)", "link": post["link"], "published": post["published"], "image": image, "summary": f'

{escape(post["text"])}

', }) return headlines
files.feeds/browser/youtube-orbital-lab/feed.y:
title: 'YouTube: Orbital Lab'
suffix: youtube-orbital-lab
# A fictional channel page (demo/sites/youtube.html, served by tools/record_demo.py) with the markup of a
# youtube.com/@channel/videos page. Its cards are drawn by a script, so youtube.hy reads it in Camoufox.
source: https://gchristensen.github.io/feedxcavator/demo/sites/youtube.html
tags: [browser]
extractor: youtube-channel
selectors:
  item: ytd-rich-item-renderer
  title: '#video-title'
  link: 'a#video-title-link'
  image: 'img'
  summary: '#metadata-line'
tasks: [browser]
files.feeds/browser/youtube-orbital-lab/youtub:
;; The simplest browser extractor in Hy: open the channel in Camoufox, wait for the video cards,
;; and read them with the selectors of feed.yaml.

(defextractor youtube-channel [feed]
  (with-browser [b]
    (-> (.open b (:source feed) :wait-for "ytd-rich-item-renderer" :scroll 1 :timeout 60)
        (.apply-selectors feed))))

files.scratch.hy:
;; Scratch: press Run to evaluate; what it prints shows below. The browser runs in the worker.

(with-browser [b]
  (setv page (.open b "https://gchristensen.github.io/feedxcavator/demo/sites/youtube.html" :wait-for "#video-title"))
  (for [title (.evaluate page "[...document.querySelectorAll('#video-title')].map(e => e.textContent)")]
    (print title)))
files.tasks.yaml:
# A feed belongs to the tasks named in its `tasks` list. A task in `run` runs as a subtask.

tasks:
  news:
    concurrency: skip

  browser:
    timeout: 600

  morning:
    run: [news, browser]

entries.name: extractor
handler
task_function
entries.doc:
@task_function("name"): registers a function for `call`, `pre` and `post` in tasks.yaml.
`pre` and `post` functions receive the task context (task, trigger, feeds, results).

entries.name: proxy
entries.doc:
proxy("name", host=, port=, user=, password=, scheme="http"): defines a proxy that feeds
(`fetch.proxy`) and fetch_url (`proxy=`) refer to by name.

entries.name: fetch_url
entries.doc:
Fetches a URL. Never raises on network or HTTP errors: returns None and records the failure,
readable through get_last_http_error() and the other accessors.

Options: method, headers, payload, `as` (html, xml, json, string, bytes; without it the raw response
is returned), charset, timeout (milliseconds), proxy (a proxy name, False for a direct connection),
follow_redirects, retry (False or a number of retries, default 2), `async` (fire and forget),
insecure (skip TLS checks), impersonate (curl_cffi browser profile), cookies.
In Python pass `as` and `async` as `as_` and `async_`.

entries.name: get_last_http_response
entries.doc: The response of the last failed fetch_url call in this request or job.

entries.name: get_last_http_error
entries.doc: The HTTP status of the last failed fetch_url call, or None.

entries.name: get_last_network_error
entries.doc: The exception of the last fetch_url call that failed on the network level, or None.

entries.name: get_last_conversion_error
entries.doc: The error raised while converting the last response (`as`), or None.

entries.name: log_fetch_errors
entries.doc: A context manager: every failed fetch inside it writes an error entry to the application log.

entries.name: browser
entries.doc:
with browser(profile="default", proxy=None) as b: takes a stealth browser from the worker's pool for the
block; in Hy, (with-browser [b :profile "default" :proxy "name"] body...). `profile` names the persistent data
directory data/browser/<profile>/ (cookies, logins); one profile is open in one browser at a time. `proxy`
names a proxy (defproxy, or `proxies` in config.yml) the browser connects through. The browser starts at the
beginning of the block and closes at its end, with its pages. In the web process (the console) the calls go
to the worker over RPC. The methods of `b` and of the pages it opens are listed in the Browser section.

entries.name: solve_captcha
entries.doc:
(solve-captcha url :profile "default" :proxy None): opens `url` in a pool browser and passes a Cloudflare
challenge there with the system mouse, so later visits with the profile (and fetch_url calls to the host) get
through. Clearance is bound to the address the challenge came from: solve it through the proxy the site is
crawled through.
A challenge may show up some time after the page opens: `watch` is how long to wait for one. True when the
page is through. In an open browser, page.solve_captcha(watch=...) does the same on that page.

entries.name: load_js
entries.doc:
(load-js "cards"): a script for page.evaluate() from a file in the directory of the workspace file that
calls it. ".js" is added to a name without a suffix. The file defines `function main()` (or
`async function main(arg)`); evaluate() returns what main returns, and `(.evaluate page js arg)` passes
`arg` to main. The file runs in a function scope of its own, so its names do not leak into the page. Names
it sets on `window` persist between calls on the same page. `:wrap False` returns the file as is. The file is read at
each call, so edits apply without a workspace reload (the workspace does not watch .js files).

entries.doc: Finds a feed by suffix, then by title.

entries.name: fetch_feed_output
entries.doc: The stored output of a background feed: {"output", "content_type"}, or None.

entries.name: store_feed_output

entries.name: store_image

write(message) or write(level, message). Level is `info` (default), `warning` or `error`.

A string is stored as is, an exception as its traceback, any other value pretty-printed.

entries.name: telegram.get_channel_messages
entries.doc:
Headlines for the most recent messages of a public Telegram channel (up to 26). The call goes
through the proxy named by `proxy` (False for a direct connection), otherwise the feed's
`fetch.proxy`, otherwise the proxy named `default` when `telegram.default-proxy` is on.

`b` is the browser bound by the block, and `page` is what b.open(url) returns:

    with browser() as b:
        page = b.open(feed["source"], wait_for="article")
        headlines = page.apply_selectors(feed)

    (with-browser [b]
      (setv page (.open b (:source feed) :wait-for "article"))
      (.apply-selectors page feed))

Each b.open opens another page; page.goto navigates the same page and returns it. Pages and the browser close
at the end of the block, so take what you need from a page inside it.

entries.name: b.open(url, wait_for=None, scroll=0, timeout=30) -> Page
entries.doc:
Opens `url` in a new page and returns it. `wait_for` is a CSS selector to wait for after the DOM
loads, `scroll` a number of scrolls to the bottom (for infinite lists), `timeout` the limit in seconds
for the navigation and for `wait_for`. Raises BrowserError when the page does not load. Later fetch_url
calls to the host reuse the browser's cookies and user agent.

entries.name: b.cookies(url=None) -> dict
entries.doc: The cookies of the browser profile as a {name: value} dict, only those sent to `url` when given.

entries.name: b.user_agent
entries.doc: The browser's user agent string (a property: `b.user_agent`).

entries.name: page.html() -> str
entries.doc: The HTML of the live DOM.

entries.name: page.url
entries.doc:
The current URL of the page, after redirects and navigations (a property: `page.url`, `(. page url)`
in Hy).

entries.name: page.selector()
entries.doc: The live DOM as a parsel selector.

entries.name: page.apply_selectors(feed=None)
entries.doc:
Applies the feed selectors to the live DOM. Parts are text content where the built-in
extractor gives inner HTML.

entries.name: page.goto(url, wait_for=None, timeout=30)
entries.doc:
Navigates the page to `url` and waits for the DOM to load, then for `wait_for` (a CSS selector) when
given. `timeout` is in seconds. Returns the page, so calls chain. Later fetch_url calls to the host reuse
the browser's cookies and user agent.

entries.name: page.click(selector, timeout=30)
entries.doc:
Clicks the first element matching `selector` (CSS, or a Playwright selector such as "text=More"),
waiting up to `timeout` seconds for it to be visible and enabled. The click is made by the driver, which
some bot checks ignore (see solve_captcha).

entries.name: page.fill(selector, value, timeout=30)
entries.doc:
Replaces the value of the input or textarea matching `selector` with `value`, waiting up to `timeout`
seconds for the element.

entries.name: page.press(selector, key)
entries.doc:
Focuses the element matching `selector` and presses `key`: a key name such as "Enter", "ArrowDown"
or "Control+A", or a single character.

entries.name: page.wait_for(selector, timeout=30, required=True) -> bool
entries.doc:
Waits for an element matching `selector`, through navigations (such as the reload a security check
does once passed). On a timeout it raises, or with `required=False` returns False.

entries.name: page.wait(seconds)
entries.doc:
Pauses for `seconds` with the page live (scripts keep running). Prefer wait_for when there is an
element to wait for.

entries.name: page.scroll(times=1)
entries.doc:
Scrolls to the bottom of the page `times` times, 0.8 seconds apart, so infinite lists load more
items.

entries.name: page.evaluate(script, arg=None)
entries.doc:
Runs a JavaScript expression in the page and returns its value. When the expression is a function,
it is called with `arg` (JSON-like data).

entries.name: page.screenshot(selector=None, type='png', quality=None, style=None, timeout=30) -> bytes
entries.doc:
The first element matching `selector`, or the viewport without one, as image bytes. Playwright
scrolls the element into view first. `type` is "png" or "jpeg" (with `quality` 0-100); `style` is CSS
applied only while the shot is taken, for example to hide fixed headers lying over the element.

entries.name: page.solve_captcha(timeout=60, attempts=2, watch=0) -> bool
entries.doc:
Passes a Cloudflare challenge on the page with the system mouse, if there is one. True when
the page is through. `watch` is how many seconds to keep looking for a challenge that has not shown yet
(it returns as soon as one does). Needs a headful browser, pyautogui and the display the browser is on.

entries.name: page.text(selector=None)
entries.doc:
The text content of the first element matching `selector` (None when nothing matches), or of the
whole document without one.

entries.name: page.close()
entries.doc: Closes the page. Pages left open are closed with the browser at the end of the `with` block.

entries.name: (defextractor name [feed] body...)
entries.doc: Defines and registers an extractor (see `extractor`).

entries.name: (defhandler name [a b] body...)
entries.doc: Defines and registers a handler. `(defhandler ^:auth name [a b] ...)` requires the API token. `(defhandler name request ...)` receives the whole request.

entries.name: (defproxy name :host ... :port ... :user ... :password ...)
entries.doc: Defines a proxy.

entries.name: (deftaskfn name [ctx] body...)
entries.doc: Defines and registers a task function for tasks.yaml.

entries.name: (with-browser [b :profile "default" :proxy "name"] body...)
entries.doc: Runs the body with a browser from the worker's pool bound to `b` (see `browser`). Both options are optional; (with-browser body...) binds `b` with the defaults. The methods are in the Browser section.

entries.name: (log-fetch-errors body...)
entries.doc: Every failed fetch inside the body writes an error to the log.

entries.name: (safe-call form)
entries.doc: Evaluates the form; on an exception prints the traceback and returns None.

entries.doc: Evaluates the form, once more if it raises. `safely-repeat3` tries three times.

entries.doc: All matches of a selector. A literal selector is checked when the file loads. Also accepts an Enlive-style vector: ($ page [:div.post :> :a]).

manual.html:
Feedxcavator manual

This manual goes from a first feed written in a few lines of YAML to feeds written in code, background tasks, browsers and custom HTTP handlers.

How Feedxcavator works

A feed is a directory under workspace/feeds/ with a feed.yaml file in it. The definition names a source (a web page, a JSON API, another feed) and says how to find headlines in it. The server serves the result at /feed/<suffix>, where the suffix is the directory name unless the definition sets another.

A feed is extracted in one of two ways:

  • On request. Each visit to the feed URL fetches the source and builds the feed again. This is the default and suits feeds that are quick to build.
  • In the background. A feed that belongs to a task is extracted when the task runs, on a schedule or by hand. The result is stored, served to everyone who visits the URL, and pushed to WebSub subscribers.

Everything you write lives as plain files in the workspace: feed definitions, Python and Hy code, task and schedule files. You can edit them in the web console, in an IDE, or keep them under git. The server notices changes to the files and reloads the workspace.

The console

The console is at http://<host>:10000/console. Its tabs:

Tab What it is for
Workspace the file tree, the editor and the output pane; feeds are created, tested and debugged here
Tasks background tasks, their feeds, and Run now
Schedules when tasks run; Run now
Runs the history of task and feed runs, with durations, headline counts and results
Subscriptions WebSub subscriptions: their feeds, callbacks, status and expiry
Word filters lists of words and regular expressions that remove headlines
Log messages written by the server and by your code
Settings the API token, the subscription URL, backup and restore, purging stored images, restart
API every function of the user library, with Python and Hy names
Manual this text

The Workspace tab

The tree on the left shows the workspace. Right-click a feed for its actions: Test, Open feed URL, Subscribe, Run feed task, Suggest selectors, New code file, Rename folder and Delete. Right-click a folder under feeds/ for New feed, and the empty part of the tree for Reload workspace. Files can be dragged to another folder.

Below the tree, the outline lists what the open file defines: extractors, handlers, functions, tasks. Click an entry to jump to it; right-click a task to run it or list its feeds.

The toolbar above the editor follows the open file. For a feed.yaml it offers Save, Test, Suggest selectors, Open (the feed URL), Subscribe and Delete. For scratch.hy it offers Run. Ctrl S saves the file, or runs it in the case of the scratch file.

Test extracts the feed without publishing it and shows the headlines in the output pane. A test skips the history filter steps, so it shows the same headlines every time and does not mark them as seen.

The header shows whether the workspace loaded. When a file fails to load, it shows the number of errors; click it to see them in the output pane. Files with errors are marked in the tree and in the editor tabs.

Ctrl K (or the search box in the header) opens a feed or a file by name.

Your first feed

Create the file workspace/feeds/my-first-feed/feed.yaml, or use New feed in the console, with this text:

title: My first feed
source: https://example.com
selectors:
  item: article
  title: h2::text
  link: h2 a
  image: img::attr(data-src)||src
pages:
  include-source: false
  path: '/page/{n}'
  start: 1
  end: 5

The feed is served at http://<host>:10000/feed/my-first-feed. Each time the URL is visited, Feedxcavator reads the pages from https://example.com/page/1 to https://example.com/page/5, finds every element matched by the item selector, and builds a headline from each of them with the other selectors, which are applied inside the item.

A link is taken from the href attribute of the matched element and an image from its src attribute, unless the selector names an attribute. The definition above takes the image from data-src, and from src when data-src is absent. Relative links are made absolute against the source URL.

Before writing selectors by hand, try Suggest selectors: it proposes a selectors block for the source page. Then press Test to see what the feed produces.

Selectors

Selectors are full CSS as implemented by parsel and cssselect: any combinator, attribute operator, :not(), :nth-child() and so on can be used. Feedxcavator adds a few things at the end of a selector:

Selector Result
h2 the inner HTML of the element (for link and image, its href or src)
h2::text the text of the element, without tags
img::attr(data-src) the value of an attribute
img::attr(data-src)\|\|src the first non-empty attribute of the list (img::data-src\|\|src also works)
:root::attr(data-id) the item element itself, written as :root
xpath://h2/a/@href an XPath expression
jmes:data.items[*] a JMESPath expression for JSON sources

When the item selector is a jmes: expression, the source is parsed as JSON, so a JSON API can be turned into a feed without code. XML sources (another RSS feed, for example) are parsed with namespaces removed.

A selector can also be a map with options:

selectors:
  item: li.post
  title: {css: 'a::text', strip: true}
  category: {css: '.tags a::text', many: true}         # a list of all matches
  published: {css: '.date::text', parse: date}         # almost any date format
  comments: {css: '.comments::text', parse: int}
  summary: {xpath: './/p[1]', parse: text}
  author: {css: '.byline::text', regex: 'by (\w+)', default: unknown}

Exactly one of css, xpath or jmes is required. regex keeps the first group of the match, or the whole match when there are no groups. Selectors are checked when the file is saved, and errors are shown with their line numbers.

Reading several pages

The pages block reads more than one page of the source. Numbered pages are built by appending path, with {n} replaced by the page number, to the source URL:

pages:
  include-source: true         # also read the URL in `source` itself
  path: '/?page={n}'
  start: 2
  end: 3
  increment: 1
  delay: 0                     # seconds between page requests

A site without page numbers can be followed through its "next" link instead:

pages:
  next: 'a.next::attr(href)'
  max: 5

source can also be a list of URLs; headlines from all of them go into one feed.

Automatic extraction

A feed with mode: auto and no selectors lets Feedxcavator work out the headlines by itself. It looks, in this order, for a feed the site already publishes, for structured data on the page (JSON-LD and microdata), and for a repeated structure of elements that looks like a list of articles. OpenGraph data is used last, because it describes the page itself rather than a list.

title: Lazy feed
source: https://example.com/blog
mode: auto
fulltext: true   # replace each summary with the main text of the linked article

fulltext: true works with selectors too. It fetches every linked page, so the feed gets slower with each headline; such feeds are good candidates for background extraction.

Filtering headlines

The filter list removes headlines. Its steps run in the order they are written:

filter:
  - history: {key: link, keep: 1000}
  - dedupe: link
  - wordfilter: {name: default, fields: [title, summary]}
  - exclude: {field: title, regex: '^Sponsored'}
  - limit: 50

history drops the headlines that the previous extractions of the feed already returned, so a feed shows only new items. key names the field that identifies a headline (link by default). The history keeps the last keep keys (1000 by default), or with keep_days the keys seen in that many days.

dedupe keeps the first of the headlines that have the same value in a field. exclude drops headlines whose field matches a regular expression; the field is title when it is not given. limit keeps the first so many headlines.

Word filters

A word filter is a named list of words and regular expressions. The wordfilter step names the filter and the fields to check; without a name the filter called default is used, and without fields only the title is checked.

Filters are edited on the Word filters tab, one entry per line. A plain word matches case-insensitively anywhere in the field. An entry written as /expr/ is a regular expression; a word boundary \b in it helps to avoid matching parts of longer words. The tab shows which feeds use each filter.

Filters can also be changed from code (for example, from scratch.hy) with add_filter_word, remove_filter_word, add_filter_regex, remove_filter_regex and list_word_filter:

(add-filter-regex "default" r"\bsponsored\b")

The same operations are available over HTTP, see Word filters over HTTP.

Fetch options and output formats

The fetch block controls how the source is downloaded:

fetch:
  backend: http                # or browser, for pages that need JavaScript
  impersonate: chrome          # the browser whose TLS fingerprint and headers are imitated
  method: GET
  headers: {Accept-Language: en}
  cookies: {name: value}
  charset: auto                # set it when the automatic detection fails
  proxy: default               # the name of a proxy from proxies in config.yml
  timeout: 30                  # seconds
  retry: 2
  wait_for: article            # browser backend: a CSS selector to wait for
  scroll: 0                    # browser backend: scroll to the bottom this many times

Requests go through curl_cffi and imitate a real browser. impersonate names the curl_cffi fingerprint (chrome by default, also firefox, safari and versioned names such as chrome124). Proxies are described in Proxies and the browser backend in Browsers.

output selects the format: rss (the default), atom, json-feed or json. RSS, Atom and JSON Feed carry the standard headline fields; plain JSON keeps every field the headlines have.

Feed definition reference

Every key is optional except source (or an extractor that does not need one). The file the console creates for a new feed lists them all as comments.

title: Feed title
suffix: feed-suffix            # the feed is served at /feed/feed-suffix; defaults to the directory name
id: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef  # keeps the stored state when the suffix changes (see "Feed identity")
enabled: true
tags: [news]                   # tasks can select feeds by tag
extends: forums/phpbb          # inherit from forums/phpbb.yaml in a group lib/ or in lib/; maps are merged
source: https://example.com    # a URL or a list of URLs
mode: selectors                # or auto
fetch:
  backend: http
  # ... see "Fetch options and output formats"
selectors:
  item: div.headline           # the container element of a headline
  title: h3
  link: a
  summary: div.preview
  content: div.body
  image: div.cover img:first-of-type
  author: div.user-name
  category: {css: 'div.category a::text', many: true}
  published: {css: 'time::attr(datetime)', parse: date}
  guid: '::attr(data-id)'
pages:
  # ... see "Reading several pages"
filter:
  # ... see "Filtering headlines"
fulltext: false                # true: fetch each linked page and use its main text as the summary
transform: function-name       # a function applied to every headline
post_process: function-name    # a function applied to the whole list of headlines
output: rss                    # rss, atom, json-feed or json
tasks: [task-name]             # extract in the background (see "Background extraction")
parallel: true                 # false: run on the sequential worker pool
websub: {enabled: true, partition: 100}  # push updates, by parts of 100 items
expect_empty: false            # true: zero headlines is normal, no zero-headline log warning or highlight in run history
extractor: extractor-name      # the code that produces the headlines instead of the selectors
params: [any additional data, [123, 456]]  # arbitrary data for the code

Any other top-level key is kept and available to code as a feed field.

Organizing the workspace

workspace/
  lib/                     shared code, loaded first (lib/_order.yaml sets an explicit order)
    forums/phpbb.yaml      a template for `extends: forums/phpbb`
  feeds/news/
    lib/                   group library: code and templates for the feeds under news/
    local/city-paper/
      feed.yaml            the feed; the directory path is its group, the directory name its default suffix
      extract.hy           feed-local code
  handlers/
  tasks.yaml
  schedules.yaml
  scratch.hy               run from the console only

Folders under feeds/ group feeds. A task can select all feeds of a group by path, and a group can share code and templates.

Templates

Feeds that read similar sites can share their common part. extends: forums/phpbb merges the feed definition into forums/phpbb.yaml: keys of the feed replace keys of the template, and maps (such as selectors or fetch) are merged key by key.

Group libraries

A group folder under feeds/ may have its own lib/ directory. Its code loads before the feeds of the group, and the feeds in the group and in its subgroups can call what it defines; other feeds do not see those names (extractors and handlers it registers are global, as always).

A group library can also hold templates. extends: base looks for base.yaml in the group libraries of the feed, nearest first, then in the workspace lib/. A template can extend a template of the same name further out, so feeds/news/lib/base.yaml may start with extends: base to refine lib/base.yaml.

Errors while loading

A broken feed file disables only that feed, and a broken group library only the feeds of its group. A broken lib/ file keeps the previously loaded workspace running. If a lib/ file fails at startup, there is no previous state to keep, so the rest of the workspace loads without that file and the error is reported.

Feed identity

A feed is identified by its suffix: it is served at /feed/<suffix>, and its stored output, history, subscriptions and run records are kept under that name. A suffix may contain ASCII letters, digits, ., -, _ and ~, and must be unique regardless of case. Without suffix: the directory name is used, so a directory whose name is not a valid suffix needs an explicit suffix.

When you change the suffix of a feed.yaml and save it in the console, the stored state moves to the new suffix. The save is refused when another feed already has that suffix. A suffix changed outside the console (in an IDE or by git) makes the feed a new one, with empty history.

id: (32 lowercase hex characters) is optional. A feed that sets one keeps its state under the id, so it survives any change of suffix or directory, and it is also served at /feed/uuid:<id>. The server never writes ids into feed.yaml itself.

Background extraction

A feed without tasks is extracted each time its URL is visited. A feed with tasks is extracted in the background: the result is stored and served when a user or a feed reader visits the URL, and pushed to WebSub subscribers. This suits feeds that need complex or slow processing.

Tasks

Tasks are defined in workspace/tasks.yaml, or on the Tasks tab. A feed belongs to a task when it lists the task in its tasks field, or when the task selects it by tag, by path or by suffix:

tasks:
  news:
    feeds: {tags: [news]}
  forums:
    feeds: {path: 'forums/*'}
  papers:
    feeds: {list: [city-paper, county-paper]}
  morning-feeds:
    run: [news, forums]           # subtasks, started together
    then: [aggregate-feeds]       # tasks started when all subtasks have finished
  aggregate-feeds:
    call: aggregate               # a task function defined in code

A task may also name pre and post task functions, which run before and after its feed jobs. timeout limits how long the task may run (written like 45s, 30m or 2h). concurrency says what happens when the task is triggered while it is still running: skip (the default) ignores the trigger, queue runs the task again after the current run, and allow starts another run at once.

Feeds with parallel: true (the default) run on a pool of parallel workers, the others one at a time on the sequential pool. worker-parallel and worker-sequential in config.yml set the sizes of the pools.

Schedules

Schedules are in workspace/schedules.yaml and are managed on the Schedules tab. They use five-field cron expressions in the local time zone unless a timezone is given. A task can be scheduled several times:

schedules:
  - task: news
    cron: '0 12 * * *'
  - task: news
    cron: '0 17 * * *'
  - task: morning-feeds
    cron: '0 7 * * *'
    timezone: Europe/Berlin

A schedule can also set enabled: false, misfire: run-once (run once when a firing was missed while the server was down; the default skip ignores missed firings), and jitter, a random delay of each firing of up to that many seconds.

A task can be started at any time with Run now on the Tasks or Schedules tab, and the tasks of a feed with Run feed task in its context menu. The Runs tab shows what ran, when, and with what result.

WebSub

Feeds announce the built-in WebSub hub at /websub in their hub link. A feed reader that supports WebSub subscribes there, and gets each new version of a background feed as soon as the task has stored it, without polling. websub: {partition: 100} in a feed sends large updates in parts of 100 items. The Subscriptions tab lists the subscriptions; it can also rewrite callback URLs in bulk, for example after the reader moved to another address.

Set websub: false in config.yml to disable the hub.

Writing code: Python and Hy

When YAML is not enough, write code. Code files sit in the workspace next to the definitions: shared code in lib/, feed-specific code in the feed directory, HTTP handlers in handlers/. A .py file is Python and a .hy file is Hy, a Lisp that compiles to Python. The Hy prelude adds a compact DSL for feed code: definition macros such as defextractor and defhandler, keyword lookup with (:title h), threading macros, and Clojure-style collection functions (assoc, update-in, group-by and others) that never modify their arguments. Python is there for those who would rather not write Lisp; the collection functions are available in it too.

Both languages can be mixed freely, even in one feed directory, because all files evaluate into one shared namespace. Hy names are translated into Python names by the usual Hy rules, so a function defined in Hy as parse-forum is called from Python as parse_forum, and a Python function clean_title is clean-title in Hy. Every Python library installed in the environment can be imported from either language.

The user library (fetching, selecting, filtering, storage, responses) is available in every file without imports. The API tab lists it with signatures in both spellings. A few names that Hy mangling cannot produce have Hy aliases: filter-history! is filter_history_update in Python, store-object! is store_object, str->html is parse_html.

Some differences to keep in mind:

  • In Python, the as and async options are passed as as_ and async_: fetch_url(url, as_="html"). In Hy they are written :as "html".
  • Hy reads :key value in a call as a keyword argument, so option values are written as strings: (fetch-url url :as "html"). For the same reason (distinct-by "link" coll) takes the key as a string.
  • (:key m) returns None for a missing key. A feed is a read-only mapping: feed["source"], feed.source and (:source feed) are the same. Hy mangles dashes in keywords, so (:image-type h) reads the "image_type" key; read a key that contains a dash with (get h "item-id").
  • Headlines are plain dicts with string keys, and assoc and the other collection functions take the keys as strings: (assoc h "title" "x"). (assoc h :title "x") does not work, because :title in a call is a keyword argument.

The scratch file

scratch.hy in the workspace root is a place to try code. It is never loaded with the workspace; Run (or Ctrl S) evaluates it in a copy of the workspace namespace and shows what it prints, or the traceback of an error, in the output pane. Use it to call a feed's functions by hand, fetch a page and try selectors on it, or change word filters.

Logging

log.write writes a string, an exception (with its traceback) or any other value to the Log tab. A level can be given as the first argument: info (the default), warning or error.

log.write("warning", f"no items at {feed.source}")

Changing headlines with code

There are three places where code can change what the selectors found, from the smallest to the largest.

A headline is a dict with these fields:

{
    "title": "Headline title",
    "link": "Headline URL",
    "summary": "Article summary (optional)",
    "content": "Full article content (optional)",
    "author": "Author name (optional)",
    "category": "A category or a list of categories (optional)",
    "image": "Image URL (optional)",
    "image_type": "image/mime-type (optional)",
    "published": "a datetime (optional)",
    "guid": "a unique id (optional)",
}

RSS, Atom and JSON Feed output ignore other fields; plain JSON output keeps all of them.

Transform

A function named in transform receives one headline and returns a changed copy, None to keep it as it is, or False to drop it:

def shout(headline):
    return {**headline, "title": headline["title"].upper()}

(defn shout [headline]
  (assoc headline "title" (.upper (:title headline))))

transform: shout

Post-process

A function named in post_process (post-process is accepted too) receives the whole list of headlines after transform and before the filter steps, and returns a new list, or None to keep the list as it is:

def by_title(headlines):
    return sorted(headlines, key=lambda h: h["title"])

post_process: by-title

The feed keeps the selectors, so when the source cannot be read it still gets the error headline that the built-in extraction produces.

Extractors

An extractor replaces the selectors altogether. The extractor field names an extractor function defined in code; a feed directory with exactly one extractor uses it even without the field. An extractor receives the feed and returns a list of headlines.

This extractor sorts the headlines found by the feed selectors by title:

@extractor("my-first-extractor")
def my_first_extractor(feed):
    headlines = parse_html_page(feed, feed.source)
    return sorted(headlines or [], key=lambda h: h["title"])

(defextractor my-first-extractor [feed]
  (sorted (or (parse-html-page feed (:source feed)) [])
          :key (fn [h] (:title h))))

Fetching and selecting in code

Fetching web resources

fetch_url (fetch-url in Hy) obtains the contents of a web resource. It does not raise on network or HTTP errors; it returns None instead. get_last_http_error returns the status code of the last failed request, get_last_http_response the whole response, and get_last_network_error the network exception. Inside a log_fetch_errors block (the log-fetch-errors macro in Hy) every failed fetch is written to the log, which helps when debugging.

The as option converts the response:

  • html: a parsed HTML document for the selector functions
  • xml: a parsed XML document
  • json: parsed JSON
  • string: the response text
  • bytes: the response body

Without it the raw response is returned. Other options include method, headers, payload, cookies, proxy, retry, impersonate and timeout, which is in milliseconds here (while fetch.timeout in feed.yaml is in seconds).

Selecting elements

Fetch a page with as_="html" and take its parts with the selector functions, which accept the selectors described in Selectors:

q(node, "div.post")              # all matches: elements, or strings for ::text and ::attr()
q1(node, "div.post h2::text")    # the first match, or None
text(node)                       # text content without tags
attr(node, "href")               # the value of an attribute
inner_html(node)                 # the HTML inside the element
outer_html(node)                 # the HTML of the element itself
extract(node, base_url=url, title="h2::text", link="a")  # one headline, as the YAML selectors build it
apply_selectors(doc, feed)       # all headlines, with the selectors of the feed

In Hy, the $ and $1 macros do the same as q and q1, and check a literal selector when the file is loaded. They also accept a selector written as a vector of keywords, where :> is the child combinator:

($ page "div.post > a")
($1 page [:div.post :> :a])
(defselectors post-parts :item "article" :title "h2::text" :link "h2 a")
(post-parts page)                ; headlines

Proxies

Proxies are defined by name under proxies in config.yml, either as a URL or as a mapping:

proxies:
  default: socks5://127.0.0.1:1080
  work:
    scheme: http          # http (the default), https, socks5, socks5h or socks4
    host: proxy.example.com
    port: 3128
    user: me              # optional
    password: secret      # optional

In the URL form, special characters in the user name and password must be percent-encoded. Changes take effect after a restart.

A fetch uses the proxy named by its proxy option, otherwise the one named by fetch.proxy of the current feed. proxy=False forces a direct connection. A name that is not defined means a direct connection, without an error.

The name default is not applied to feeds by itself; a feed must name it in fetch.proxy. Telegram calls use the fetch.proxy of the calling feed too (or their own proxy argument); when the feed names none, they go through the proxy named default only if telegram.default-proxy is true. The /forward links made by forward_url(url, referer, proxy="name") fetch through the named proxy. WebSub callbacks never use a proxy.

Browsers

Pages that need JavaScript can be opened in a real browser, either with fetch.backend: browser in the feed or from code:

with browser() as b:
    page = b.open(feed.source, wait_for="article", scroll=3)
    headlines = page.apply_selectors(feed)

(with-browser [b]
  (-> (.open b (:source feed) :wait-for "article")
      (.apply-selectors feed)))

A page can also be driven: goto, click, fill, press, wait_for, wait, scroll, evaluate (with load_js for scripts kept in files), screenshot, html, text and url. The Browser section of the API tab describes every method of the browser and the page.

Browsers run in the worker; code in the web process (the console) reaches them over the local RPC. Each with browser() block starts a browser and closes it at the end.

After a page is opened, later fetch_url calls to the same host reuse the browser's cookies and user agent (kept in memory by the process until it restarts), so a browser can pass a challenge and plain fetches can do the rest.

The browser does not use the proxies defined in config.yml: fetch.proxy has no effect on fetch.backend: browser.

Profiles

A profile is a named, persistent browser data directory, data/browser/<profile>/, which keeps cookies, local storage and logins between runs. Profiles need no definition: a new name creates its directory on first use. Choose one with browser(profile="shop") or (with-browser [b :profile "shop"] ...); the default is default, and fetch.backend: browser always uses default. One profile can be open in one browser at a time, so jobs on the same profile wait for each other even when the pool has room.

To log in to a site once, open the profile headful (browser-headless: false), log in by hand, and later runs reuse the session. chrome-profile.sh [profile] [url] opens Chrome with a pool profile for the patchright and playwright engines, and firefox-profile.sh [profile] [url] opens Camoufox for the camoufox engine. Close the window before the worker uses the profile.

Profiles are per engine: cookies and sign-ins saved by Chrome do not carry over to camoufox. Use a new profile name (or clear the folder) when switching engines, and sign in again.

Security checks

Sites behind a security check (DDoS-Guard, a bot check of their own) show the content only after the check passes and reloads the page, which can take ten seconds or more. Wait for the content rather than for a fixed time: page.wait_for(selector, timeout, required=False) keeps waiting through the reload and returns False on a timeout instead of raising, so the code can reload once or give up. The clearance cookies stay in the profile, so usually only the first page of a run waits.

Cloudflare challenges

(solve-captcha url :profile "default") opens a page in a pool browser and passes a Cloudflare challenge on it (the "Just a moment..." page or a Turnstile checkbox); in an open browser, (.solve-captcha page) does the same for that page. Both return True when the page is through.

Turnstile ignores clicks the browser driver makes, so the real pointer is moved and clicked with pyautogui: three moves to random points at least 15% of the screen away from its edges, then a click on the checkbox, and a second try when the challenge stays. The checkbox is found in the page, not at fixed screen coordinates: its place comes from the widget's box, and page coordinates are mapped to the screen by moving the pointer over the page and reading where the page saw it. captcha-position is the fallback when no widget is found. One solve runs at a time, since there is one pointer.

This needs pyautogui and a headful browser on a display the worker can reach, with the window not covered by others:

python3 install.py --with-captcha

On Linux, when the worker runs as another user than the desktop session, allow it on the desktop display with xhost + (or xhost +SI:localuser:<user>) and set browser-display: ":0". Under Xvfb the clicks work too, but nobody can watch them. Set captcha-flash: true to see where the pointer acts while checking a setup.

Browser settings

The browser is set up in config.yml:

Key Default Meaning
browser-engine camoufox camoufox (Firefox based), patchright or playwright
browser-channel chrome the installed browser patchright or playwright drives; the bundled Chromium when it is missing
browser-pool-size 1 how many browsers may run at once; further jobs wait
browser-headless see below true or false; by default headful on Linux when a display or Xvfb is available, otherwise headless
browser-display none Linux: the X display the worker uses when DISPLAY is not set, such as ":0"
captcha-position none [x, y]: the screen point solve-captcha clicks when it cannot find the Turnstile widget
captcha-flash false solve-captcha shows a marker at each point the pointer moves to

Engine and channel are global; profiles cannot set their own. Changes take effect after a restart, because the browser pool lives in the worker process.

On Linux without a display the worker starts Xvfb, when it is installed, so the browser runs headful, which is less detectable than headless. Install it with the distribution's package (xorg-x11-server-Xvfb on Fedora/RHEL, xvfb on Debian/Ubuntu). browser-headless: true forces headless mode.

Browser engines

Engine Browser Setup
camoufox (default) a Firefox build with fingerprint spoofing install.py --with-browser
patchright the installed Chrome (browser-channel), patched against automation detection install.py --with-browser=patchright
playwright stock Playwright Chromium, no stealth install.py --with-browser=playwright

No engine is installed with the core package. install.py installs the chosen ones into the virtual environment and downloads their browsers: the Camoufox build (kept in the user's cache folder, outside the venv), or for patchright and playwright their Chromium when no Chrome is installed. It then test-launches Camoufox; on Linux a failure there usually means missing system libraries (GTK 3, libX11-xcb, ALSA), which the distribution's firefox package brings in. Several engines can be installed at once (--with-browser=camoufox,patchright); the one in use is browser-engine, and switching it needs a restart. If the engine set there is not installed, a browser feed fails with "browser-engine is patchright, but it is not installed".

With camoufox, each profile keeps one fingerprint for the host's OS in data/browser/<profile>/feedxcavator-fingerprint.json, created on the first launch, so the sign-in script and the worker present the same browser. The file also keeps the host GPU that Camoufox reads by starting a bare browser for a moment (a short extra window), so this happens once per profile, normally in firefox-profile.sh. Delete the file to get a new identity, or after changing the machine's graphics.

Telegram

telegram.get_channel_messages(channel) returns headlines for the latest messages of a public Telegram channel, and telegram.notify(message, chat_id) sends a text message. Both need api-id and api-hash under the telegram key of config.yml and a one-time login with python -m feedxcavator telegram-login.

Handlers

Handlers define a custom web API for your feeds. A handler registered with the name my-first-handler is called when http://<host>:10000/handler/my-first-handler is visited. Its arguments receive the query or form parameters of the same names. A handler whose only argument is called request receives the whole request instead (method, path, headers, body, params, json).

A handler returns one of the response functions (text_page, json_page, web_page, redirect_to and others), a dict or list that is sent as JSON, or None for an empty response.

@handler("my-first-handler")
def my_first_handler(param):
    log.write(param)
    return text_page("OK")

The API token

With auth=True (^:auth in Hy) the request must carry the API token in the x-feedxcavator-auth header. The token is generated on the Settings tab. It is stored hashed and shown only once, so copy it when it appears.

This handler gives the stored output of a background feed to an external program and takes the processed output back:

(defhandler ^:auth my-secure-handler request
  (setv feed (find-feed "kitty-site"))
  (if (= (:method request) "GET")
      ;; return the stored kitty feed for external processing
      (do (setv output (fetch-feed-output feed))
          (web-page (:content-type output) (:output output)))
      ;; store the externally processed output
      (do (store-feed-output! feed {"content_type" "application/json"
                                    "output" (.decode (:body request) "utf-8")})
          (text-page "OK"))))

Word filters over HTTP

The REST API at /api/wordfilter/<action> changes word filters from outside the server. The actions are list, list-words, add-word, remove-word, add-regex and remove-regex; each takes a JSON body and the API token. The author uses these commands for the iShell browser extension.

Examples

Fetch new threads from a set of bulletin board forums. The params field of the feed holds the numeric ids of the forums, and the feed selectors describe the thread list of a forum page.

(defextractor bb-extractor [feed]
  (lfor forum (:params feed)
        :setv forum-url (+ (:source feed) (str forum))
        ;; stage 1: thread links from the forum page, without the ones seen before
        thread (filter-history! forum-url (or (parse-html-page feed forum-url) []))
        ;; stage 2: the first post of every thread
        :setv page (fetch-url (:link thread) :as "html")
        (do (log.write (+ "visited: " (:link thread)))
            (assoc thread
                   "title" (html-unescape (:title thread))
                   "image" (q1 page ".post_text img::attr(src)")
                   "summary" (outer-html ($1 page ".post_text"))))))

Extract data from a JSON API. The params field holds the user id.

API_TOKEN = "..."

@extractor("json-api-extractor")
def json_api_extractor(feed):
    url = f"https://json.api/method/data.get?user_id={feed.params}&access_token={API_TOKEN}&v=1"
    posts = get_in(fetch_url(url, as_="json"), ["response", "items"], [])
    headlines = [{"title": p.get("title"),
                  "link": p.get("url"),
                  "summary": p.get("text"),
                  "image": get_in(p, ["attachments", "photo_640"]) or get_in(p, ["attachments", "photo_320"])}
                 for p in posts]
    return sorted(headlines, key=lambda h: h["link"] or "", reverse=True)

Transform another RSS feed and turn its titles upper case. The selectors read the XML, and a transform function changes the titles, so no extractor is needed:

title: Loud feed
source: https://example.com/rss.xml
selectors:
  item: item
  title: title::text
  link: link::text
  summary: description::text
transform: shout

(defn shout [headline]
  (assoc headline "title" (.upper (:title headline))))

A task function that runs after the morning feeds:

@task_function("aggregate")
def aggregate(ctx):
    log.write(f"aggregating after {ctx['trigger']}")

Hostnames: a reader on the same machine

The server is reached from two directions: browsers follow the links written into feed items, and a WebSub subscriber talks to the hub and is pushed updates. When the reader runs on the same machine and the machine's LAN name resolves to itself there, one address serves both.

Example: Feedxcavator and NewsSharp, a web feed reader, run on a machine called lab. People read news in a browser on other computers of the LAN. NewsSharp subscribes to Feedxcavator over WebSub.

port: 21000
host: 0.0.0.0                     # listen on the LAN too, not only on 127.0.0.1
hostname: 'http://lab:21000'      # websub-hostname and secure-hostname default to it
#secure-hostname: 'https://lab:22000'   # only with an HTTPS reverse proxy, see HTTPS in the README
  • hostname is the base of image, redirect and forward links in feed items, of each feed's self link and of its hub link (http://lab:21000/websub). Browsers on the LAN and NewsSharp on lab can all open it.
  • In NewsSharp, add feeds by the same address, for example http://lab:21000/feed/city-paper, so the subscription URL equals the feed's self link. Feeds without tasks, which are extracted when NewsSharp polls them, then also get lab links: during a request the server writes links with the address the request came to.
  • NewsSharp chooses the callback URL and sends it with the subscription. Feedxcavator opens it from lab to verify the subscription and to push updates, so it may use localhost or lab. If the callback cannot be opened, the subscription is not verified and the log shows "WebSub verification failed".

Check that the name resolves on the server itself (ping lab there). If it does not, add 127.0.0.1 lab to the hosts file, or keep hostname at lab and set websub-hostname: 'http://localhost:21000'. With the second option, subscribe at the localhost URL. A feed without tasks that NewsSharp polls at localhost then gets localhost image links, which do not open on other computers.

Maintenance

The daily service task (service-task in config.yml) deletes stored images and log entries older than max-age-days, and prunes old history and run records. Run records are kept for run-history-days days.

The Settings tab downloads a backup of the database, optionally with the workspace, and restores one; the workspace of a backup is unpacked only into an empty workspace directory. The tab can also purge stored images and restart the server when it runs under the supervisor or the systemd unit. Child processes (browsers) are stopped on shutdown; when the server is killed forcibly, the children it left behind are stopped on the next start.

When repl-port is set (or FEEDXCAVATOR_REPL_PORT), the worker opens a Python/Hy REPL bound to 127.0.0.1 that shares the namespace of the workspace code.
